645.title: Behold the man (John 18:39–19:16)
645.hook: purple robe, thorns, and Pilate's words: behold the man
645.howItsDone: Christians remember this scene in Holy Week and in the Stations of the Cross, and in Jerusalem pilgrims walking the Via Dolorosa pass a Roman-era arch known as the Ecce Homo Arch.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Pilate asked what is truth? and walked out before the answer. Did you stay for someone's answer? Day six hundred forty-five.

A crown of thorns. A purple cloak. A Roman official beside a beaten man, one hand stretched toward him, as if presenting him to a crowd below. Sometimes the prisoner holds a reed like a scepter. Sometimes the crowd is painted in too, shouting. Painters have come back to this scene again and again for more than five hundred years, and many of the paintings carry the same two-word Latin title. Today, the moment they come from, and the two words.

Pilate offers the crowd a choice: there's a custom of releasing one prisoner at Passover. Shall I release the King of the Jews? They shout for Barabbas instead, and John adds four words: "Now Barabbas was a robber." Then Pilate has Jesus scourged. Roman soldiers twist thorns into a crown, throw a purple robe on him, the color of emperors, and mock him: hail, King. They strike him. And then Pilate brings him out. In the King James Bible: "Then came Jesus forth, wearing the crown of thorns, and the purple robe. And Pilate saith unto them, Behold the man!" In Latin, Ecce homo. Why does Pilate say it? Perhaps he means, look at him, he's harmless, he's been punished enough. Perhaps it's contempt. The text doesn't tell us. But John's readers have heard more in it than Pilate could have meant. Behold the man: here is what a human being looks like, stripped, mocked, and still standing. Many Christians hear in it every person who has ever been beaten, humiliated or put on display, and God standing with them. The scene keeps tightening. Pilate says again, I find no fault in him. The chief priests cry, crucify him. Pilate is afraid. He tries once more to release him. Then they warn him that letting this man go would make him no friend of Caesar. Near noon, Pilate brings Jesus out a last time: behold your King. And the chief priests answer, we have no king but Caesar. Then Pilate, the Roman governor, hands him over to be crucified by Roman soldiers.

Here's the practice: look at human suffering without turning away. Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who is suffering right now. Someone you know, or a face from the news you scrolled past. Don't analyze it. Don't fix it. Just look, the way Pilate made the crowd look. Notice the urge to glance away, and stay a little longer. If you pray, you can hold that person before God in silence. If you don't, simply let them be seen by you for these minutes. The bell holds the time.
Ecce homo. Latin for behold the man: Pilate's words as he brings out Jesus, crowned with thorns and robed in purple.
Your line: behold the man. Today, when you see someone suffering, in person or on a screen, pause and really look before you move on. Day six hundred forty-five.

646.title: The seamless robe (John 19:17–24)
646.hook: soldiers gamble for his coat, woven in one piece
646.howItsDone: Christians remember the dividing of Jesus's garments in the Stations of the Cross, and in some churches on Maundy Thursday the altar is stripped bare, which some link with this scene.

segments.voice: Yesterday, thorns and purple, and Pilate's ecce homo. Your line was behold the man. Who did you really look at? Day six hundred forty-six.

The soldiers on duty keep what the condemned man leaves behind. That's how John tells it: at the foot of the cross, four soldiers are dividing up Jesus's clothes. They split them into four shares, one each. Four men, four piles of cloth, and a job to get through. And then they come to one piece they don't want to cut. John doesn't describe the nails here. He lingers on this: a garment, and a game of chance.

First, John sets the scene. Jesus goes out "bearing his cross" to the place of a skull, in Hebrew, Golgotha. He's crucified between two others. Pilate has a sign fixed above him, Jesus of Nazareth, the King of the Jews, written in Hebrew, Greek and Latin, so anyone passing can read it. The chief priests ask him to change it to he said he was king. Pilate refuses: "What I have written I have written." Then the clothes. In the King James Bible: "now the coat was without seam, woven from the top throughout." Woven in one piece, top to bottom, no stitching. The soldiers say, let's not tear it; let's cast lots for it. And John says this fulfilled a line of the Psalms: "They parted my raiment among them, and for my vesture they did cast lots." That's Psalm twenty-two, a psalm that begins in anguish and ends in praise, and Christians have long read it alongside the crucifixion. Why does John care about a robe? He doesn't say. Readers have offered answers for centuries. The Jewish historian Josephus describes the high priest's tunic as woven in one piece, so some readers see Jesus here as a priest. Early church writers, like Cyprian of Carthage, saw the robe as a picture of the church: one piece, which even the soldiers wouldn't tear. And some just see the cruel ordinariness of it: men gambling at the foot of a cross while a man dies above them. All three can sit together. The text simply gives us the robe, and leaves it with us.
screen: `WHAT I HAVE WRITTEN I HAVE WRITTEN.`
`ONE PIECE, NO SEAM, TOP TO BOTTOM.`
`PRIEST, CHURCH, OR A GAMBLE AT A CROSS?`
then, large: `WOVEN FROM THE TOP THROUGHOUT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: give away a piece of clothing. Settle, and breathe. Picture your closet or your drawers. Somewhere in there is something warm and good that you haven't worn in a year. A coat, a sweater, a pair of shoes. Picture it, and picture someone who could use it this week: a shelter, a coat drive, a neighbor, a friend's kid. Let yourself feel the little tug of not wanting to let go. Then let it go, in your mind first. If you pray, you can offer it as a small gift. The bell holds the time.
The seamless robe. Jesus's coat, woven in one piece from the top, which the soldiers wouldn't tear, and gambled for instead.
Your line: woven from the top. Today, actually bag up the piece of clothing you pictured, and put it by the door so it leaves the house. Day six hundred forty-six.

647.title: It is finished (John 19:25–30)
647.hook: his mother, the beloved disciple, I thirst, and it is finished
647.howItsDone: On Good Friday many churches hold services around Jesus's last words from the cross, sometimes called the Seven Last Words, gathered from all four Gospels; three of them come from John.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a coat with no seam, and soldiers casting lots. Your line was woven from the top. Did the clothing make it out the door? Day six hundred forty-seven.

While the soldiers gamble, a few people are standing near the cross. John names them. His mother. His mother's sister. Mary the wife of Cleophas. Mary Magdalene. And the disciple whom Jesus loved. The other men who followed him are nowhere in John's scene. These few stayed. And from the cross, in the little breath he has left, Jesus speaks to them. In John's Gospel, he says only three things from the cross. Today, all three.

The first is to his mother and his friend. In the King James Bible: "Woman, behold thy son!" And to the disciple: "Behold thy mother!" And from that hour, John says, that disciple took her unto his own home. Dying, he makes sure his mother will have a home. Christians read it in more than one way. Read plainly, it's simple, faithful care. Catholic and Orthodox Christians also hear Mary given as mother to the church, with the beloved disciple standing for every follower. The second saying: "I thirst." The man who offered a woman at a well living water, and said whoever believes in him will never thirst, is thirsty. Someone lifts a sponge of sour wine to him on a branch of hyssop, the plant used at the first Passover to mark the doorposts. Then the third. "When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost." In Greek, it is finished is one word: tetelestai. It comes from telos, the end, the goal, the point toward which something has been moving. It doesn't mean it's over, I'm done for. It means it's complete, accomplished, brought to its goal. Just before, John uses the same verb: Jesus, knowing that all things were now accomplished. Christians have heard this one word as the heart of what they believe the cross achieved. Different churches describe that achievement in different words: a debt paid, a victory won, love shown to the end. Each of those readings hears completion, not defeat. And then: he bowed his head. John makes it sound like a choice. He handed over his spirit.

Here's the practice: finish one thing and rest. Settle, and breathe. Think of one small thing you've left half done. A text you never sent. A drawer half sorted. A thank-you note. A form. Not the big project. Something you could actually finish today. Picture yourself completing it, and then stopping. Not grabbing the next thing. Just resting in done. If you pray, you can offer that small completion to God. If you don't, simply notice how good finished feels. The bell holds the time.
It is finished. One word in Greek, tetelestai: not it's over, but it's complete, brought to its goal.
Your line: it is finished. Today, finish the small thing you pictured, and then take five minutes to rest before starting anything else. Day six hundred forty-seven.

648.title: Blood and water (John 19:31–37)
648.hook: a spear, and the eyewitness insists: he saw it
648.howItsDone: Some Christians see the blood and water as signs of Communion and baptism, and Catholic devotion to the Sacred Heart and the Divine Mercy image both draw on this moment.

segments.voice: Yesterday, one Greek word from the cross, tetelestai. Your line was it is finished. What did you finish, and did you rest? Day six hundred forty-eight.

John usually tells his story in a calm, steady voice. Then, right after the death of Jesus, the narrator suddenly does something unusual. He steps forward, almost into the frame, and speaks straight to you. I'm not making this up, he says, in effect. Someone saw it. And he's telling you so that you will believe. It's like a documentary where the person holding the camera turns it around for a moment. Today, what he insists he saw.

It's the day of preparation, and the next day is a Sabbath, and a high day. The bodies can't be left on the crosses into it. So the authorities ask Pilate to have the legs broken and the bodies taken down. Soldiers break the legs of the two men crucified with Jesus. Then they come to him. In the King James Bible: "But when they came to Jesus, and saw that he was dead already, they brake not his legs: But one of the soldiers with a spear pierced his side, and forthwith came there out blood and water." Then comes that unusual line: "And he that saw it bare record, and his record is true: and he knoweth that he saith true, that ye might believe." Bare record means testified. The Greek verb is martyreo, to bear witness. It's where our word martyr comes from: a martyr was first of all a witness. Why does John stress this so hard? Some early Christians taught that Jesus only seemed to have a body, and only seemed to die. Some scholars think John is answering that: real spear, real wound, real death, and someone was standing there. John also hears two scriptures. A bone of him shall not be broken: the rule for the Passover lamb. And from the prophet Zechariah: they shall look on him whom they pierced. Then there's the blood and the water itself. John doesn't explain it. Early church writers like Augustine and John Chrysostom saw in it the two great signs of the church: the water of baptism and the blood of Communion. Others read it as simple evidence of death. The text leaves it there, with a witness.
screen: `A HIGH DAY: LEGS BROKEN, BUT NOT HIS.`
`REAL BODY, REAL DEATH, A REAL WITNESS.`
then, large: `HE THAT SAW IT BARE RECORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: honor what witnesses tell you. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone who has told you about something they saw or lived through, and you didn't quite take it in. A grandparent's war story. A friend's account of how they were treated. A coworker who said something was wrong. Bring their face to mind and hear their words again, slowly, as if they were telling the truth, because they may have been. If you pray, you can give thanks for them. If you don't, simply honor them in your mind. The bell holds the time.
Blood and water. What flowed from Jesus's side when the soldier's spear pierced it, and what the eyewitness insists he saw.
Your line: he who saw it. Today, ask someone to tell you about something they witnessed, and listen to the end without correcting them. Day six hundred forty-eight.

649.title: A hundred pounds of myrrh (John 19:38–42)
649.hook: Nicodemus, who came by night, comes by day with spices
649.howItsDone: Christians remember Jesus's burial on Holy Saturday, a day of quiet waiting in many churches, and Orthodox Christians honor Joseph and Nicodemus among the myrrh-bearers on the second Sunday after Easter.

segments.voice: Yesterday, a spear, blood and water, and a witness who insisted. Your line was he who saw it. Whose story did you listen to? Day six hundred forty-nine.

Way back in chapter three, a man came to Jesus at night. His name was Nicodemus, a Pharisee, a leader, a respected teacher. He came after dark, and he asked careful questions about being born from above, and the last we hear from him that night is a puzzled one: how can these things be? In chapter seven, he spoke up once, briefly, saying the law should give a man a hearing. And then he disappeared from the story. Now Jesus is dead. Peter, the loudest of the followers, is nowhere in this scene. And two quiet men walk forward, in daylight, to do what nobody else will.

The first is Joseph of Arimathea. John says he was a disciple, "but secretly for fear of the Jews." In John's Gospel, that phrase usually means the religious authorities, and the other Gospels say Joseph sat on their council. Now he goes to Pilate himself and asks for the body. That's a public act. Then the second man. In the King James Bible: "And there came also Nicodemus, which at the first came to Jesus by night, and brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about an hundred pound weight." A hundred pounds. John's pound, the Roman litra, was lighter than a modern pound, but even so, that's an enormous amount of spice. The Hebrew Bible tells of a king of Judah laid in a bed filled with spices. Some readers see Nicodemus and Joseph giving Jesus a royal burial, for the King of the Jews, as Pilate's sign said. They wrap the body in linen with the spices, as John says was the Jewish custom of burial. And there's a garden near the place of the crucifixion, and in it a new tomb where no one had ever been laid. It's close by, the Sabbath is coming, so there they lay him. Notice the arc of this man's story. He came by night in chapter three. He spoke up once in chapter seven. Now he comes by day, carrying something heavy, in front of everyone. John never tells us what Nicodemus believed in the end. Tradition makes him a saint. The text simply shows a man coming slowly into the light.
screen: then, large: `WHICH AT THE FIRST CAME TO JESUS BY NIGHT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: show your care openly. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you care about, or a cause, or a belief, that you've kept a little quiet. Maybe you love someone and haven't said it out loud lately. Maybe you agree with someone who's being criticized and haven't said so. Maybe you've kept your faith, or your questions, to yourself. You don't have to make a speech. Just picture one small way to carry your care into the daylight. If you pray, you can ask for some of Nicodemus's courage. The bell holds the time.
A hundred pounds of myrrh. The spices Nicodemus carried in daylight, enough for a king's burial, for the man he first visited by night.
screen: `A HUNDRED POUNDS OF MYRRH — today's word`.

segments.voice: Your line: in daylight now. Today, take the one small step you pictured, and let your care be seen. Day six hundred forty-nine.

650.title: Running to the tomb (John 20:1–10)
650.hook: Peter and the other disciple race; the linen cloths lie folded
650.howItsDone: John 20 is read in many churches on Easter morning, and in some places Christians mark Easter with sunrise services, gathering outdoors before dawn as Mary did.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Nicodemus came by day with a hundred pounds of myrrh. Your line was in daylight now. How did you let your care be seen? Day six hundred fifty.

In a museum in Paris hangs a painting from 1898 by the Swiss artist Eugène Burnand. There's no tomb in it, no angel, no risen Jesus. Just two men running, at dawn, side by side, hair blown back. One is older, gripping his chest. The younger one leans forward, hands clasped, eyes wide. You can almost hear their breathing. Of all the resurrection scenes he could have painted, Burnand chose the run. And so does John. Before anyone sees anything, two friends run.
screen: `NO TOMB, NO ANGEL. JUST THE RUN.`

segments.voice: It starts with Mary Magdalene. In the King James Bible: "The first day of the week cometh Mary Magdalene early, when it was yet dark, unto the sepulchre, and seeth the stone taken away from the sepulchre." She doesn't think resurrection. She thinks robbery. She runs to Peter and the disciple Jesus loved: "They have taken away the Lord out of the sepulchre, and we know not where they have laid him." And then the race: "So they ran both together: and the other disciple did outrun Peter, and came first to the sepulchre." It's such a human detail. Readers have smiled at it for centuries: the beloved disciple, who many believe is the source behind this Gospel, can't resist mentioning that he won. But he stops at the entrance. He stoops, looks in, sees the linen cloths lying there, and doesn't go in. Peter arrives, out of breath, and walks straight in. He sees the linen cloths, and the cloth that had been around Jesus's head, not with the others, "but wrapped together in a place by itself." That's an odd detail for grave robbers. Thieves don't unwrap a body and leave the wrappings neatly behind. Then the other disciple goes in too, "and he saw, and believed." Believed what, exactly? John adds, honestly, that they didn't yet understand the scripture that he must rise. Something had shifted in him before he understood it. And then, strangely, they both just go home. No announcement. The great news of Easter begins with a race, an empty room, folded cloth, and two men walking home not quite sure what they've seen.
screen: `HE SAW, AND BELIEVED, NOT YET KNOWING.`
then, large: `SO THEY RAN BOTH TOGETHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: run to good news. Settle, and breathe. Think about the last time someone told you good news. Did you run toward it, or did you say that's nice and go back to your screen? Now think of someone in your life with good news right now: a new job, a recovery, a baby, a small win. Picture yourself going to them, not walking, running, the way these two ran. If you pray, you can give thanks for their good news. If you don't, simply let yourself be glad for them. The bell holds the time.
Running to the tomb. Peter and the beloved disciple racing at dawn, and finding the cloths left behind.
Your line: they both ran. Today, when you hear someone's good news, go to them quickly and celebrate it with them, before anything else. Day six hundred fifty.

651.title: Rabboni (John 20:11–18)
651.hook: Mary turns at her name, and becomes the apostle to the apostles
651.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Mary Magdalene on July 22, and Orthodox Christians honor her as equal to the apostles; many churches read this passage during the Easter season.

segments.voice: Yesterday, two friends racing at dawn. Your line was they both ran. Whose good news did you run toward? Day six hundred fifty-one.

The two men have gone home. Mary Magdalene hasn't. She's standing outside the tomb, crying. She stoops and looks in, and there are two angels in white, sitting where the body had been, one at the head and one at the feet. They ask her: woman, why are you weeping? And she answers as if angels were the most ordinary thing in the world, because grief is louder than wonder. They have taken away my Lord, and I don't know where they've laid him. Then she turns around, and someone is standing there.
screen: `TWO ANGELS, AND GRIEF LOUDER THAN WONDER.`

segments.voice: She doesn't recognize him. John says she supposed him to be the gardener. And she asks: sir, if you've carried him off, tell me where, and I'll take him away. Then one word. In the King James Bible: "Jesus saith unto her, Mary. She turned herself, and saith unto him, Rabboni; which is to say, Master." Her name. That's all it takes. Back in chapter ten, he said the good shepherd calls his own sheep by name, and they know his voice. Here it happens. John stops to translate it for his readers: Master, teacher. He says her name; she answers with the word she knew him by. Then he says something people have puzzled over: "Touch me not; for I am not yet ascended to my Father." In Latin, noli me tangere, and painters loved it. The Greek may mean something closer to stop clinging to me, don't hold on: there's somewhere to go and a message to carry. And he gives her the message. Go to my brothers. So she goes, and in the Greek she says it in her own voice: I have seen the Lord. She's the first person in John's Gospel to see the risen Jesus, and the first sent to tell. Christian tradition calls her the apostle to the apostles, the one sent to those who would be sent. In 2016, Pope Francis raised her day, July twenty-second, to a full feast. Orthodox Christians call her equal to the apostles. One more thing worth clearing up: the idea that Mary Magdalene was a reformed prostitute isn't in the Gospels. It grew from a sixth-century sermon that merged her with other women. The Gospels themselves remember her as a witness. This week: thorns and purple, a seamless robe, it is finished, blood and water, myrrh, a race, and now a name.
screen: then, large: `I HAVE SEEN THE LORD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say I have seen the Lord, or as much of it as is true for you. Settle, and breathe. Remember being called by name by someone who loved you. A parent at the door. A friend across a crowded room. Hear your own name in their voice. Then, if you're a Christian, you can say Mary's words quietly: I have seen the Lord. If you're not, think of something good you've seen with your own eyes this week, and say it out loud: I have seen that. The bell holds the time.
Rabboni. My teacher, my master: what Mary says when she hears her name and turns.
Your line: I have seen the lord. Today, use someone's name warmly, on purpose, and tell one person about something good you've seen. Day six hundred fifty-one, and another week on the path.

she supposes he's the gardener, until he says her name.

fork.setup: you're Mary, weeping at the tomb. a man you take for the gardener asks why you're crying. what do you say?
options: sir, if you've carried him off, tell me where, and I'll take him.
fork.reveal: she asks the gardener for the body, and then he says one word: Mary. she turns: Rabboni.

original.note: Greek spelling of a Semitic word that John translates as master, teacher.

trapdoor: what you thought: Mary calls him teacher.
what it means: grief so loud she mistakes him for the gardener, until he says her name, and she's the first one sent to tell.
what a scholar hears: rabbouni, Aramaic, and the Latin 'apostola apostolorum', apostle to the apostles. the 'penitent prostitute' idea comes from Gregory the Great's homily of 591, not the Gospels.

sources.ref: Decree of the Congregation for Divine Worship (3 June 2016)
